articles.contentSnippet:
Article URL: https://github.com/tamnd/riemann-handbook
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50596664
Points: 55
# Comments: 26
articles.fullContent: A book, in PDF and EPUB, that writes the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis in tamnd/riemann-lean as mathematics: definitions, theorems, lemmas and their proofs, in words. The claim is not checked. Nobody has built the Lean project in full yet, and no person has checked the written statements against the Lean code. This book explains the Lean code. It is not a separate check of the mathematics. See What is checked. The volumes Volume Source 0 Guide: how to read, the status of the claim, notation, the named results, the index of Lean names content/front/ and tamnd/riemann 1 Background: the mathematics that the proof uses, in 17 chapters the Learn pages of tamnd/riemann 2 The proof: the top of the proof, its chapters and steps the written proof of tamnd/riemann 3 to 12 The Lean development, one branch or one Lean folder in each volume content/dev/, written for this book The books are in the releases. The plan of the development volumes Each declaration of the proof is inside the dominated subtree of exactly one other declaration (its immediate dominator, in the graph of uses from riemannHypothesis). The ledger gives an entry to each declaration whose dominated subtree is large, in tiers: 1,000 or more declarations (591 entries), 300 or more (1,927), 100 or more (5,764). It assigns each entry to a volume by its branch of the proof or by its Lean folder, and to a chapter by its Lean folder. In a chapter, the entries come from the top of the proof down. python -m rhb ledger --records /path/to/records --min 1000 --write ledger/coverage.md has the numbers. prompts/entry.md is the brief for the writers of entries. Build You need Python 3.11 or later, pandoc 3.8 or later and Tectonic. Put tamnd/riemann and tamnd/riemann-lean next to this repository. pip install . python -m rhb survey python -m rhb check python -m rhb build --volume 0,1,2 --formats pdf,epub The books go to build/. The pipeline is that of The Handbook of Algorithms: Markdown, then pandoc with filters/rhb.lua, then LaTeX with tex/handbook.sty, then Tectonic. The EPUB is EPUB 3 with MathML. articles.title: Fast-Anything: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow
articles.contentSnippet:

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50596155
Points: 46
# Comments: 28
articles.fullContent: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow. Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway. fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible. Install npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything # or: cargo install fast-anything Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain (rustup). Use fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py # or: -- node app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c Or step by step: command what it does scan -- <cmd> profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are port [id] records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + TASK.md verify release-builds the port and replays every recorded call enable / disable swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte) bench times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs report markdown + SVG card for your PR doctor checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents --agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use. Proof, not vibes That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time. Results Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from examples/. app before after Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) 4.91s 42ms, 116× TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) 3.11s 155ms, 20× PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) 2.94s 53ms, 55× Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) 3.02s 144ms, 21× Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) 3.13s 228ms, 14× C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 4.03s 312ms, 13× Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) 3.50s 1.18s, 3× (11× on the function; the rest is JVM startup) C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) 431ms 127ms, 3.4× C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) 3.02s 1.09s, 2.7× fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×. Why not rewrite it all? Compile time: each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes. Cache: every port shares one .fast/target. Delete it whenever you like. Risk: your code stays as it is. Rust is opt-in per function, checked against real behavior. articles.summary: Le projet open source fast-anything propose une approche d'optimisation ciblant uniquement les 5 % de fonctions lentes d'une application au lieu de tout réécrire en Rust. L'outil profile l'application, enregistre des centaines d'appels réels, délègue le portage de la fonction à un agent de codage (Claude, Codex) et vérifie la stricte équivalence des résultats avant d'intégrer le module Rust. L'intégration est réversible à tout moment et s'adapte à de nombreux langages source (Python, Node, Go, Java...).

articles.fullContent: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News. The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images|Getty ImagesThe first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”➡️ Skip the lot. articles.fullContent: Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them. These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below. As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions: Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations. Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure. Notified all potentially affected customers. The following work is underway: We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis. We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties. We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review. We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it. articles.fullContent: Credits Anil Seth won the 2025 annual Berggruen Prize Essay Competition for his English-language essay, “The Mythology Of Conscious AI.” A neuroscience professor and the director of the Centre for Consciousness Science at the University of Sussex, Seth is also the co-director of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research Program on Brain, Mind and Consciousness. He wrote, “Being You: A New Science of Consciousness” (Dutton, 2021). For centuries, people have fantasized about playing God by creating artificial versions of human beings. This is a dream reinvented with every breaking wave of new technology. With genetic engineering came the prospect of human cloning, and with robotics that of humanlike androids. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) is another breaking wave — potentially a tsunami. The AI systems we have around us are arguably already intelligent, at least in some ways. They will surely get smarter still. But are they, or could they ever be, conscious? And why would that matter? The cultural history of synthetic consciousness is both long and mostly unhappy. From Yossele the Golem, to Mary Shelley’s “Frankenstein,” HAL 9000 in “2001: A Space Odyssey,” Ava in “Ex Machina,” and Klara in “Klara and The Sun,” the dream of creating artificial bodies and synthetic minds that both think and feel rarely ends well — at least, not for the humans involved. One thing we learn from these stories: If artificial intelligence is on a path toward real consciousness, or even toward systems that persuasively seem to be conscious, there’s plenty at stake — and not just disruption in job markets. Some people think conscious AI is already here. In a 2022 interview with The Washington Post, Google engineer Blake Lemoine made a startling claim about the AI system he was working on, a chatbot called LaMDA. He claimed it was conscious, that it had feelings, and was, in an important sense, like a real person. Despite a flurry of media coverage, Lemoine wasn’t taken all that seriously. Google dismissed him for violating its confidentiality policies, and the AI bandwagon rolled on. But the question he raised has not gone away. Firing someone for breaching confidentiality is not the same as firing them for being wrong. As AI technologies continue to improve, questions about machine consciousness are increasingly being raised. David Chalmers, one of the foremost thinkers in this area, has suggested that conscious machines may be possible in the not-too-distant future. Geoffrey Hinton, a true AI pioneer and recent Nobel Prize winner, thinks they exist already. In late 2024, a group of prominent researchers wrote a widely publicized article about the need to take the welfare of AI systems seriously. For many leading experts in AI and neuroscience, the emergence of machine consciousness is a question of when, not if. How we think about the prospects for conscious AI matters. It matters for the AI systems themselves, since — if they are conscious, whether now or in the future — with consciousness comes moral status, the potential for suffering and, perhaps, rights. It matters for us too. What we collectively think about consciousness in AI already carries enormous importance, regardless of the reality. If we feel that our AI companions really feel things, our psychological vulnerabilities can be exploited, our ethical priorities distorted, and our minds brutalized — treating conscious-seeming machines as if they lack feelings is a psychologically unhealthy place to be. And if we do endow our AI creations with rights, we may not be able to turn them off, even if they act against our interests. Perhaps most of all, the way we think about conscious AI matters for how we understand our own human nature and the nature of the conscious experiences that make our lives worth living. articles.fullContent: Raph Levien, November 21, 2026 This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI. Rust GUI is still compelling The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative. Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia. The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance? For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things. Native is complicated My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria. I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front. While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems. Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. articles.fullContent: LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage. On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site. The code is under the MIT license. LookAtMyQuant 2: Qwen3.5-4B in 1.2 GB LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai. The recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time. The recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release, packed for the Apple Silicon runtime. articles.fullContent: gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go code, using TinyGo. Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a SQL function: gopgext writes the C glue, the install script and the control file.Experimentalgopgext is experimental. Don’t use it in production: a bug in the generated code or the Go runtime runs inside the server, where it can crash it or corrupt data, and the API and generated SQL may change without notice.Just GoA project is plain Go files. The standard library works: fmt, regexp, encoding/json, crypto/*, maps, generics, iterators, defer/recover.Types map to SQLStrings, numbers, arrays, NULLs, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON map to SQL types. Define your own data types and composite types in Go.Queries and errorsRun SQL through SPI, return errors with SQLSTATE codes, log, read settings and stay responsive to query cancellation.Beyond functionsWrite triggers, aggregates, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST and BRIN operator classes, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks.Proven on contribPorts of PostgreSQL’s contrib modules (pgcrypto, hstore, pg_stat_statements, cube, …) pass upstream’s regression tests.Safe coexistenceSeveral Go extensions load in one backend. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL memory.Hello, world#package main import ( "strings" "gopgext/pg" ) // Hello returns a greeting for name. // //gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe func Hello(name string) string { return "Hello, " + name + "!" } // Shout upper-cases s. An empty string raises an error. // //gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe func Shout(s string) (string, error) { if s == "" { return "", pg.Errorf(pg.CodeInvalidParameterValue, "nothing to shout") } return strings.ToUpper(s) + "!", nil } func main() {} // runs once per backend, when PostgreSQL loads the library gopgext init hello # creates hello/go.mod and hello/main.go gopgext install hello # builds hello.so, hello.control, hello--1.0.sql and installs them psql -c 'CREATE EXTENSION hello' -c "SELECT hello('world')" # hello # --------------- # Hello, world! The tutorial walks through it step by step.A sibling project#gopgext uses the same approach as gokm, which builds Linux kernel modules from Go: a custom TinyGo target and runtime layer for the host, a C runtime compiled by the host’s own build system (PGXS here, kbuild there), and generated glue.

articles.fullContent: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

articles.fullContent: Turn on the wall plug, hold the power button on, and the PC starts. We will be understanding the flow of electric power from wall socket, to your computer to the point when first instruction is fetched. Unraveling the components, hand-offs in between. Lets rewind it. And follow the electricity from the wall socket. Cool? Nah, that doesn't seem enough, let's rewind it back more, and follow the electricity when we don't even power the wall plug on. Every-time you unplug the PC, and then plug it back in - It shows the correctly configured time, how is it keeping track of time without any power? Clue: It does have power, just not from the wall. Enter > CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) batteries. A small battery inside every computer, which always stays on when the wall plug is off. Also called the coin-cell battery. A standard coin battery (example model number - CR2032) delivers a nominal voltage of 3V, and a continuous current of a few microamps. What if I remove the battery, or my PC stays in the garage for 10 years? Well, the things that this battery keeps alive will go out. The internal clock, and sometimes a few BIOS settings (on legacy motherboards). And when you turn on the PC, the clock will show some weird fixed date like 1 Jan 1960. Alright, we'll keep the battery then. What happens now? The clock is okay, where is the main electricity? Let's turn on the wall plug, this will send the real power down to the PC. We press the power button... Wait, how would the PC know I pressed the power button, who will detect this power button press - if THIS is the button that gives power? Enter > The standby power line. This is a power line (a wire) that gets the electricity as soon as you turn on the wall plug (it does not care about you pressing the PC's power button). It is a 5V line, and it is called a standby rail (rail is just a synonym to a wire here, I've seen "rail" being used much more than wire), therefore the name of this rail - 5VSB (5V stand-by). A pretty standard power line you would find on any PC, this powers up a few critical circuits, that should be always on. Including the one watching your power button. wait, wait, wait. I studied that wall power is AC at 220V or 110V, but here we just jumped to from wall to 5V line, how did that happen? Enter > PSU (power supply unit), ah, this one is a heavy and chunky piece of the PC. PSU has several components, and will be our major point of discussion for a while. PSU converts the power from high-voltage AC to low-voltage DC. PSU also makes sure that the DC power is stable, constant, and precisely delivered (meaning no ups and downs in voltage), PC components need constant, stable and precise low-voltage DC power to function. Keeping the internals of a PSU for another article, what we need to remember is, PSU takes in 220V/50Hz AC power and gives out 5VSB rail. This awesome circuit, does a lot of things (hence the name "SUPER"), at some point of time in history, engineers gathered all small-small low level circuits, and combined their functionalities into this one single chip now called the Super IO. It does stuff like reporting and regulating the low-level stuff which touches our physical world - fan speeds, temperature, voltages, etc. And this is the circuit that detects our power button press. By the way, this circuit runs on 3.3 Volts. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50597159
Points: 1

articles.fullContent: A read-only drift report for your cloud infrastructure. It finds resources that someone changed or deleted outside your Terraform, OpenTofu or CloudFormation code, and resources that exist in your account but no state file or stack knows about. It ranks them by severity and explains each one in plain English. AWS Azure, GCP, OCI Terraform / OpenTofu drift ✅ ✅ (any provider plan -refresh-only can refresh) CloudFormation drift ✅ — Resources not in any IaC ✅ planned It ships four ways, from the same code: a command-line tool (cloud-drift-report) a Claude skill (Claude Code, Claude desktop and claude.ai) a Cursor skill, plus a Cursor rule for older versions a GitHub Action (orchesterra/cloud-drift-report@v0) It never writes to AWS or to Terraform state, sends no telemetry and needs no account. Built by OrchesTerra. This free tool is a one-off check from your laptop or CI. OrchesTerra is the cloud platform that runs it continuously across all your AWS accounts and fixes what it finds, with approvals. Try the live demo (no sign-up) or see what it does. What it checks Source How Terraform / OpenTofu Runs plan -refresh-only -lock=false into a temporary plan file and reads it with show -json, or reads a plan JSON you already have. CloudFormation Runs drift detection on the stacks you name (or every stack in a region), waits for it, then reads the resource drifts. Not in IaC Lists the account (about 170 resource types, mostly through the AWS Cloud Control API) and compares it with your Terraform state files and CloudFormation stacks. Anything neither lists is reported. For each drifted resource you get the address, type, action (changed or deleted outside IaC), each changed attribute (before → after), a severity, and a short "what probably happened". For each resource not in IaC you get its name, region, type, ID or ARN and a severity. The not-in-IaC scan skips what AWS creates itself: default VPCs and their subnets, route tables and security groups, service-linked roles, AWS-managed keys and policies, and resources another AWS service owns (an EKS cluster security group, an RDS-managed secret, instances launched by an Auto Scaling group). They are counted in the report's coverage line but not listed as findings. Types it could not list (access denied, or the type needs a parent resource) are named in the JSON output, so you know what was not checked. Severity High: security relevant. Security groups and rules, NACLs, IAM, bucket policies, public access, ACLs, encryption, KMS, resource policies, passwords. Medium: any other change that alters behaviour, deleted resources, and most resources not in IaC. Low: tags only, and log groups an AWS service created for one of your resources. Formats: Markdown (default), CSV, JSON and a self-contained HTML page (no external assets, light and dark mode, severity filter). Install You need Python 3.10+. The CloudFormation and not-in-IaC modes also need boto3; Terraform mode needs tofu or terraform on PATH. Command-line tool pip install cloud-drift-report Or the latest code from GitHub: pip install git+https://github.com/orchesterra/cloud-drift-report. Or run the script directly with no install: python3 skills/cloud-drift-report/scripts/drift_report.py --help Claude skill Copy the skill folder into your Claude skills directory: cp -r skills/cloud-drift-report ~/.claude/skills/ Then ask Claude: "check drift in ./infra", "make a drift report for my CloudFormation stacks in us-east-1", "what changed outside Terraform?" or "what in this account isn't in Terraform?" Cursor skill Cursor versions with Agent Skills read the same folder: mkdir -p ~/.cursor/skills && cp -r skills/cloud-drift-report ~/.cursor/skills/ For older Cursor versions, copy the rule into your project instead: mkdir -p .cursor/rules && cp cursor/rules/cloud-drift-report.mdc .cursor/rules/ Credentials The tool never asks for, stores or sends credentials. It uses whatever is already set up on the machine, through the standard AWS credential

articles.fullContent: A book, in PDF and EPUB, that writes the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis in tamnd/riemann-lean as mathematics: definitions, theorems, lemmas and their proofs, in words. The claim is not checked. Nobody has built the Lean project in full yet, and no person has checked the written statements against the Lean code. This book explains the Lean code. It is not a separate check of the mathematics. See What is checked. The volumes Volume Source 0 Guide: how to read, the status of the claim, notation, the named results, the index of Lean names content/front/ and tamnd/riemann 1 Background: the mathematics that the proof uses, in 17 chapters the Learn pages of tamnd/riemann 2 The proof: the top of the proof, its chapters and steps the written proof of tamnd/riemann 3 to 12 The Lean development, one branch or one Lean folder in each volume content/dev/, written for this book The books are in the releases. The plan of the development volumes Each declaration of the proof is inside the dominated subtree of exactly one other declaration (its immediate dominator, in the graph of uses from riemannHypothesis). The ledger gives an entry to each declaration whose dominated subtree is large, in tiers: 1,000 or more declarations (591 entries), 300 or more (1,927), 100 or more (5,764). It assigns each entry to a volume by its branch of the proof or by its Lean folder, and to a chapter by its Lean folder. In a chapter, the entries come from the top of the proof down. python -m rhb ledger --records /path/to/records --min 1000 --write ledger/coverage.md has the numbers. prompts/entry.md is the brief for the writers of entries. Build You need Python 3.11 or later, pandoc 3.8 or later and Tectonic. Put tamnd/riemann and tamnd/riemann-lean next to this repository. pip install . python -m rhb survey python -m rhb check python -m rhb build --volume 0,1,2 --formats pdf,epub The books go to build/. The pipeline is that of The Handbook of Algorithms: Markdown, then pandoc with filters/rhb.lua, then LaTeX with tex/handbook.sty, then Tectonic. The EPUB is EPUB 3 with MathML. articles.contentSnippet: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 1:37 PM PST · November 21, 2026 Image Credits:Matthias Balk/picture alliance / Getty Images Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI. Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.” Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS. That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.” Newsletters Subscribe for the industry’s biggest tech news Related Latest in Apps

articles.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
articles.contentSnippet: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup — in a trend that's already popular in China. Experts question the long-term consequences if this becomes a trend in Hollywood, too.
articles.fullContent: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, big batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.The two 18 Pro phones aren’t just different sizes; the Pro Max also benefits from a faster chip and better main camera sensor.The rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. articles.title: Muru
articles.fullContent: 21st November 2026 - Link Blog Muru. Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.
